clue.text: Balanced, like 1984 not 2001

definitions.meaning: level, equal on both sides, as a balanced score is
1984 divides by two with nothing over, while 2001 leaves a remainder, so only the first is this kind of number

explanation.surface: A remark that Orwell's year is more harmonious than Kubrick's space odyssey.
explanation.definitionFit: A level, equal contest or scale is balanced; numbers divisible by two get the same word.

clue.text: Simple sailor friend of Mesty

definitions.meaning: in Captain Marryat's novel Mr Midshipman ..., the young midshipman Jack is befriended by Mesty (Mesty is Mephistopheles, an Ashanti sailor)

explanation.surface: A naive seaman who is a companion of a character called Mesty.
explanation.walkthrough: Mesty is the former slave who befriends the hero of Marryat's 1836 sea novel; the hero's surname supplies the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something simple is effortless, requiring no skill or labour.

clue.text: Bezel, beaten thin, fashioned for a popular heroine

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape or make, so the letters of the preceding words are shaped into something new

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A jeweller hammers the rim of a ring thin to make something for a favourite character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beaten' looks like an anagram signal but is fodder; 'fashioned' does the work on all fifteen letters of BEZEL BEATEN THIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice heroine is among the best-loved characters in English fiction.

clue.text: Judge not soft on film like Cats (according to Eliot)

indicators.note: the clue reads 'Judge, not soft': the judge stands in where the soft letter was in the word for film

parts.note: a pellicle is a thin skin or film
p (piano) means soft in music

explanation.surface: A judge who is no softie about the movie version of the musical Cats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' signals the swap: take PELLICLE, a thin film, and put J (judge) where P (soft) was. Cats the musical draws on Eliot's Old Possum poems.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliot's Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats describes the black-and-white Jellicle breed, so the word describes his cats.

clue.text: European revolutionary detailed in Gage's memoir

indicators.note: de-tailed, with the tail cut off, so the final letter of the revolutionary goes

parts.note: Lenin led the Russian revolution of 1917

explanation.surface: A continental radical whose life is set out at length in a memoir by Gage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' seems to mean 'described', but it is read as de-tailed: LENIN loses his last N. Nicholas Gage's 1983 memoir is named after his mother, killed in the Greek Civil War.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicholas Gage's book about his mother's execution by Greek communist guerrillas bears her first name as its title.

clue.text: A king relinquishing his last field

indicators.note: the king gives up his own final letter, so the closing letter of that name is dropped

parts.note: Lear is Shakespeare's king, who gives away his realm

explanation.surface: A monarch handing over the last of his land, as Lear divided his kingdom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'relinquishing his last' fits Lear's story, but it drops the R that ends LEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A poetic word for a meadow or open grassland.

clue.text: Formal wear, old fashioned perhaps, on grooms

parts.note: an Old Fashioned is a whisky cocktail, so 'perhaps' marks it as one example
to groom someone is to tidy or dress them

explanation.surface: Wedding clothes look dated on the bridegrooms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old fashioned' reads as 'out of date', but it is the Old Fashioned drink, an example of a mixed drink; 'on' joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Evening frocks worn to smart parties are a standard item of semi-formal attire.

clue.text: Steinbeck's work notes feed a novel

indicators.note: novel as an adjective means new, so the letters of the preceding words are made new by rearranging

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Steinbeck's notes supply material for one of his novels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like part of the literary picture, but here it is an adjective meaning new, signalling an anagram of NOTES FEED A.
explanation.definitionFit: John Steinbeck's 1952 novel of the Salinas Valley carries this title.

clue.text: Old woman caught by stupid attack upset a Scottish poet

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother, a person's old woman
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the two words before it are read from bottom to top

parts.note: dim means stupid
a raid is an attack

explanation.surface: A mother caught up in a foolish assault that upset a Scots writer.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'upset' turns the whole of 'stupid attack' upside down at once; Hugh MacDiarmid was the pen name of Christopher Grieve.
explanation.definitionFit: Hugh MacDiarmid was the pen name of C. M. Grieve, the leading figure of the twentieth-century Scottish literary renaissance.

clue.text: Cold prince agreed to host British tribe of early ironsmiths

parts.note: C stands for cold, as on a tap
Prince Hal is the young Henry V in Shakespeare

indicators.note: a host takes in a guest, so the word for agreed contains the letter for British

parts.note: yes expresses agreement

explanation.surface: An aloof prince agreed to entertain a British tribe of ancient metalworkers.
explanation.walkthrough: The ancient people of the Black Sea coast were famed in Greek sources as the first ironworkers.
explanation.definitionFit: Greek writers credited this people on the southern Black Sea coast with inventing iron-working.

clue.text: Around India, don't speak against a deity

indicators.note: the pieces after it are placed around the letter for India

parts.note: sh is the call for silence
V, for versus, means against
I is India in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone in India told to hush for speaking out against a god.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' signals that SH, V and A go round I (India), giving SH-I-VA.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hindu god of destruction and renewal, one of the principal gods of the faith.

clue.text: Monarch, recently chief, flanked by his high priests

indicators.note: to be flanked is to have something on either side, so his goes on both sides of what precedes it

parts.note: taken as written
ER (Elizabeth Regina) was the most recent queen, the monarch until 2022
arch means chief, as in archenemy

explanation.surface: A king who recently took charge, surrounded by his senior clergy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recently' tells you the monarch is the late Queen Elizabeth, abbreviated ER (Elizabeth Regina); 'flanked by' splits the word for his around the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Those at the top of a priestly order are chief priests in a church hierarchy.

clue.text: One poet or another mostly covered by Orwell (Eric originally)

indicators.note: covering surrounds something, so the writer's real surname encloses the trimmed poet

parts.note: George Orwell was the pen name of Eric Blair

indicators.note: most of the word is used, losing its final letter

parts.note: another poet, W. H. Auden

indicators.note: the first letter of the name is taken

explanation.surface: A remark that a poet or two is largely discussed by Orwell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One poet or another' seems a single vague phrase; 'One poet' defines, 'or' links, and 'another' is AUDEN, cut to AUDE and put in BLAIR, then E from Eric.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Baudelaire wrote Les Fleurs du mal, the landmark French collection of 1857.

clue.text: English men argue vigorously about a Bulwer-Lytton book

indicators.note: a vigorous argument stirs things up, so the letters of the words around it are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Englishmen hotly debating a novel by Bulwer-Lytton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' links the pieces; 'vigorously' shuffles MEN ARGUE plus A, after E.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Bulwer-Lytton's 1832 novel tells of an eighteenth-century schoolmaster hanged for murder.

clue.text: Twain, once excessively recited

indicators.note: something recited is spoken, so the letters entered match the sound of the word for excessively

parts.note: too means excessively, as in too much

explanation.surface: Mark Twain once read his work at too great a length.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twain' looks like Mark Twain, but it is the old word meaning a pair, so 'once' marks it as archaic.
explanation.definitionFit: Twain is an archaic word for a pair, the number after one.

clue.text: A lesser creed in America than Asia nowadays

annotationWithheld.clue: A lesser creed in America than Asia nowadays

clue.text: Article by essayist. Poem by Blake

parts.note: the is the definite article
Charles Lamb wrote the Essays of Elia

explanation.surface: A piece by an essayist, plus a poem by William Blake.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Lamb, author of the Essays of Elia, was Blake's contemporary; 'by' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the Songs of Innocence, the pastoral poem beginning 'Little Lamb, who made thee?'

clue.text: Start including posh Eastern dance

indicators.note: the word for start takes in the letter for posh

parts.note: to begin is to start
U means upper-class, posh

explanation.surface: To start, a smart dance from the Orient.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class is old British slang for posh. 'Start' is the verb BEGIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A Caribbean ballroom dance in bolero rhythm, made famous by the song Begin the Beguine.

clue.text: Majority of Hamlet's role in Hamlet?

definitions.meaning: the greater share of something, most of it
the title character has the finest, meatiest acting role in Shakespeare's play, the one every actor wants

explanation.surface: A question about how much of the play the Prince of Denmark occupies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Majority' means the larger share; the second reading treats the title role as the choicest in the play.
explanation.definitionFit: Most of something is its larger share; the lead in a tragedy is the plum role.

clue.text: Helle's father's book removed from islands around Troy

indicators.note: the shortened islands go around the letter for troy weight
the letter for book is taken out of the islands

parts.note: the Bahamas are an Atlantic island group
t abbreviates troy, the weight used for precious metals

explanation.surface: A Greek father's book taken from islands near Troy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Troy' suggests the Trojan isles, but it gives t, the abbreviation for troy weight; BAHAMAS less B goes round it.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the king of Boeotia fathered Phrixus and Helle, who fell from the golden ram into the Hellespont.

clue.text: Is backing I need badly, postponed indefinitely?

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the letters of the word before it are reversed

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the letters are rearranged badly

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asking whether their cause is shelved forever after they badly need support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' looks like support but signals reversal; 'badly' signals the anagram, and the phrase is Latin, meaning without a day.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latin legal phrase, 'without a day', used of a meeting adjourned with no date fixed.

clue.text: Be taken out by a playwright for a drink

indicators.note: the two letters are removed from the dramatist's name

parts.note: Edward Albee wrote Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?
taken as written

explanation.surface: Being taken out for a drink by a dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken out for a drink' is the surface; really BE is taken out of ALBEE.
explanation.definitionFit: A beer-like brew, a common pub drink.

clue.text: Lillian Flynn's work is not brightened by plants

parts.note: something not lit up is dark
to plant is to put or set, so plants means puts down

explanation.surface: A novelist's book that is not lit by any greenery.
explanation.walkthrough: Gillian Flynn's 2009 thriller is meant; the OCR reads Lillian. 'plants' is a verb, sets down, not vegetation.
explanation.definitionFit: Gillian Flynn's second novel, the thriller between Sharp Objects and Gone Girl.

clue.text: Le Carr's arms dealer guy, Romeo

parts.note: a guy is a rope holding a tent
R is Romeo in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Le Carré's weapons dealer is a lover-boy, a real Romeo.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Roper, villain of The Night Manager. 'guy' means a tent line, not a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Roper is the arms trafficker the hero infiltrates in John le Carré's The Night Manager.

clue.text: Composer a miser uncovered

indicators.note: with its cover stripped away, the word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: Silas Marner is George Eliot's miserly weaver

explanation.surface: A composer revealed as a skinflint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a miser' is a particular one, Silas Marner, from George Eliot's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Arne wrote the music of Rule, Britannia!

clue.text: Wrongdoer beheaded outside stronghold. Quickly, perhaps?

indicators.note: the shortened wrongdoer goes outside, around, the stronghold
losing its head, the word drops its first letter

parts.note: a sinner does wrong
a keep is a castle's central tower

explanation.surface: A criminal executed outside a fortress, and fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quickly' looks like an adverb but is Mistress Quickly, hostess of the Boar's Head tavern in Shakespeare; 'perhaps' marks her as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Mistress Quickly keeps the Boar's Head tavern in Shakespeare's history plays, so she is an example of a landlady running a tavern.

clue.text: Old character: at last he played Noah

indicators.note: played around with, so the picked letters are rearranged
at last takes the final letters of the following words, at, he and Noah

explanation.surface: An elderly actor finally took the role of Noah.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old character' sounds like a veteran actor, but it is an Old English letter; 'last' takes T, E and H, which 'played' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: A letter used in Old English and Icelandic for the th sound.

clue.text: Gods a rebel rejected

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the word for rebel is reversed

parts.note: to rise up is to rebel

explanation.surface: The gods were spurned by a rebel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rebel' is the verb RISE (as in rise up), and 'rejected' turns it round after A.
explanation.definitionFit: The principal group of Norse gods, including Odin and Thor.

clue.text: Ten other plays at a crime scene — where's Macavity?

definitions.text: at a crime scene — where's Macavity?

indicators.note: the letters play about, moving into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Ten more dramas staged at a murder scene, with Eliot's mystery cat missing.
explanation.walkthrough: In Eliot's poem Macavity the Mystery Cat is never present when a crime is found: that is the poem's refrain.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliot's refrain says the cat is always absent from where a crime has just happened.

clue.text: Girl interested in squalor points to this compiler

parts.note: E and S, east and south, are compass points
the setter calling themselves me

explanation.surface: A girl drawn to filth points at the setter.
explanation.walkthrough: Salinger's story For Esmé — with Love and Squalor gives the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Salinger's story is addressed to a girl named in its title alongside love and squalor.
